summary: A note from MIT-DMCG on Host 106 saying it now offers the Echo and Discard services from RFC 347 and 348 on sockets 7 and 9. It describes its choices: refusing a connection if the machine is too busy and aborting after two idle minutes. It asks whether a random character generator service would also be useful.

plainLanguage.summary: A school says its computer now has two test services running. It also asks people whether they would like a third, one that makes up random letters.

subtitle: MIT-DMCG announces daemon processes for testing network connections.

tldr.problem: Network developers needed simple services to test whether connections worked correctly and to validate protocol implementations.
tldr.mechanism: MIT-DMCG implemented the Echo and Discard services from RFCs 347 and 348 as daemon processes on host 106, available on sockets 7 and 9.
tldr.outcome: Sites could test their connections by sending data and comparing what came back, or by sending data that would be silently discarded.

today: RFC 361 documents the implementation of two foundational test services that became standard utilities on the early ARPANET for validating network connections and protocol implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 361 is a brief announcement from Bob Bressler at MIT-DMCG (MIT's Distributed Computing Message Group) that Host 106 now offers the Echo and Discard test services defined in RFCs 347 and 348. These services are accessible on sockets 7 and 9.
sections.plainLanguage: MIT has set up two testing services on the network that anyone can use to check if their connection works.

sections.title: Service Behavior
sections.content: The RFC describes two administrative choices for how the services behave. First, if the host is too full to support another daemon process, it will refuse the connection by sending a CLS (close) message. Second, if no activity occurs for two consecutive minutes (no data received or output blocked), the connection will be aborted.
sections.plainLanguage: If the machine is too busy, it says no. If nothing happens for two minutes, it hangs up to save resources.

sections.title: Possible Future Services
sections.content: Bressler asks the network community whether a third service would be useful: a random character generator. He notes that many systems offer such a utility on their login connections, but putting it on its own network port would let anyone use it without logging in. He suggests it would be useful for testing new NCP implementations and for gathering network statistics.
sections.plainLanguage: The author asks if people would like a third service that just sends random letters. This would help test software and collect data about how networks work.
